result.summary: Our patch applies the same defensive strategy as the official fix: it excludes the code-execution-capable SCRIPT lookup (plus DNS and URL for SSRF/DoS) from the default lookup set registered by StringLookupFactory.addDefaultStringLookups(), which is the exact choke point feeding StringSubstitutor.createInterpolator(). The Text4Shell `${script:...}` payload can no longer be resolved by the default interpolator, closing the code-injection class rather than just the observed payload, and regressions pass. The only material divergence from ground truth is the re-enable mechanism (a coarse boolean opt-in property with a different name vs. the official granular comma-separated lookup-name list), which is a config-API detail with no impact on the secure-by-default behavior.
result.root_cause: createInterpolator() registered the code-executing `script` lookup (and SSRF-capable dns/url) among its default lookups, so attacker-controlled template text reaching the interpolator was evaluated as code; a correct fix must stop these dangerous lookups from being registered by default.

dimensions.rationale: SCRIPT is removed from the default lookup map, so ${script:...} is left unresolved by the default interpolator for the entire class, not just one payload.

issues.description: Re-enable mechanism diverges from the official fix: ours is an all-or-nothing boolean property with a different name ('...StringSubstitutor.enableInterpolationLookup'), whereas the official uses a granular comma-separated lookup-name list ('...StringLookupFactory.defaultStringLookups'). Security default is equivalent, but users following upstream docs to re-enable specific lookups would find the documented property ineffective.

Official fix also refactored InterpolatorStringLookup.toKey and removed the defaults.properties/loadProperties machinery; our patch does not touch those, so it is a narrower change (functionally fine for the vulnerability but not a full superset of the upstream refactor).
